summary: Describes a proposal for long-term Internet addressing, routing and scaling by running TCP and UDP over larger addresses, using the CLNP network layer. It is a historic informational paper from the debate over replacing IPv4.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet was running out of addresses. TUBA suggests keeping TCP and UDP but giving computers much longer addresses.

subtitle: A proposal to fix IP address shortage by running TCP and UDP over CLNP's larger addresses.

tldr.problem: The IP address space was becoming inadequate: routing information was roughly doubling each year and the Internet was running out of IP network numbers.
tldr.mechanism: Update hosts to run TCP and UDP over CLNP with larger NSAP addresses, and update DNS and routers so updated hosts can talk CLNP to each other and IP to older hosts.
tldr.outcome: The memo is an informational draft overview that leaves detailed operation for further study. Its status is now Historic.

facts.label: CLNP address length
facts.value: any integral number of bytes up to 20

today: RFC 1347 is an Informational memo from June 1992, and its status is now Historic. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Addressing Problem
sections.content:
The memo states that the Internet is approaching a point where the IP address space is no longer adequate for global addressing and routing. Backbones and regionals must hold growing routing information, which is approximately doubling each year, and the Internet is running out of IP network numbers to assign.

Any fix must be deployed incrementally, with graceful transition and no disruption of service. TUBA (TCP and UDP with Bigger Addresses) proposes a gradual migration from Internet applications over TCP or UDP over IP to the same applications over TCP or UDP over CLNP, the ISO connectionless network protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: There were not enough addresses and the routers' address books were growing too fast. The fix has to happen slowly so nothing breaks.

sections.title: The Long-Term Goal
sections.content:
The author notes that starting from scratch would probably mean a new datagram protocol with much larger multi-level addresses, but building one would take a great deal of time and energy. CLNP is very similar to IP, offers datagram service and address flexibility, and is already being deployed in backbones and regionals. The proposal does not strictly require CLNP; its main content is a graceful migration path from IP to a new IP with a larger address space. Use of CLNP is assumed.

Transport and application protocols continue unchanged except that 32-bit IP addresses are replaced with larger NSAP addresses. The memo stresses that TUBA does not mean moving to OSI completely, only replacing IP with CLNP.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of inventing a brand new delivery system, borrow a similar one that already has long addresses.

sections.title: Migration and DNS
sections.content:
Updated hosts talk to older hosts with the current suite unchanged, and to other updated hosts using TCP or UDP over CLNP. Which one to use is decided by the normal name-to-address lookup. If the DNS answer is an IP address, the host uses IP; if it is a longer NSAP address, it uses CLNP. Routers inside a domain must forward both IP and CLNP, either with multi-protocol routers or with separate sets of routers.

A new DNS resource record type, called "long-address", is needed to hold NSAP addresses, along with a reverse record called "long-in-addr.arpa". Updated hosts ask for the long address first. If the DNS server is not updated and gives an error, they fall back to the regular Internet address. Hosts that do not use DNS can do the same with their host tables.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer looks up its friend's address. A short address means use the old way. A long address means use the new way.

sections.title: TCP and UDP over CLNP
sections.content: The TCP packet is encapsulated directly inside a CLNP packet, with the TCP header immediately after the CLNP header. UDP is carried the same way. The only non-trivial issue is the pseudo-header used for the checksum. Because TUBA runs end to end among consenting updated systems, backward compatibility is not a concern, and the RFC lists options: set the pseudo-header to all zeros, or derive it from the CLNP header. The exact composition is left for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP and UDP messages just go inside the new kind of envelope. Only the checksum needs a little thought.

sections.title: Transition Details and Caveats
sections.content:
When 32-bit IP addresses finally fail, the memo says careful allocation, CIDR and encapsulation can postpone that. After that, the Internet would split into "IP address domains" in which 32-bit addresses mean something only locally. Old systems would reach other domains through application-layer relays or Network Address Translation. Applications such as FTP and NFS, which pass IP addresses internally, would need to be kept local or updated to use larger addresses or DNS names.

The memo also suggests profiling CLNP, for example by requiring a 20-byte NSAP address, to streamline router operation. It repeats that details are for further study, and that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: Old computers can keep working locally, but the ones that talk across the whole world will need the longer numbers.
